newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar at lowest ebb since 1988.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar at lowest ebb since 1988.

text.p: With the central bank turning a blind eye, the Taiwan dollar on Wednesday succumbed to the U.S. dollar's worldwide strength and plunged to its lowest level against the greenback since 1988.

Analysts said, however, that despite its tumble, Taiwan's currency was not suffering from -- nor particularly vulnerable to -- the kind of speculative attacks that have shocked several southeast Asian currencies in July.

The local unit, hounded by intense selling pressure all day, ended sharply lower for the second consecutive session, closing at T$28.480 on Wednesday against Tuesday's already sharply depreciated T$28.170 finish.
The T$28.480 finish was the Taiwan dollar's lowest since it ended at T$28.490 on October 29, 1988.
Turnover through dealers was active at US$344.5 million.

The central bank on Tuesday allowed the Taiwan dollar to fall below T$28 for the first time since 1989, opening a floodgate for local dollar selling amid the greenback's strength against the yen and other major currencies.
"The U.S. dollar continued to be strong (on Wednesday), and the central bank continued to let the market go. The result is another big fall," said one dealer at a foreign bank.
Analysts said the Taiwan dollar was far from the kind of de facto devaluations that speculators have forced on to currencies like the Thai baht and Philippine peso.

"Taiwan's central bank is purposely letting the Taiwan dollar fall. The central banks of Thailand and the Philippines had no choice but to let their currencies plunge," said Daniel Chen, chief economist at Chinatrust Commercial Bank.
"Taiwan's central bank can easily reverse the rate if it wants to. It is that powerful," Chen said.
The bank has been seen by experts as tacitly welcoming, even encouraging, a depreciation in the interest of stronger exports -- Taiwan's economic life-blood.
They say Taiwan's central bank, boasting foreign exchange reserves of over US$90 billion, could easily defend the currency as it often has at times of political uncertainty.

The bank's strength was never clearer than during a long stretch in 1995-96 when it held Taiwan's dollar above T$27.5 despite military menacing by rival China that triggered a run on foreign exchange and gold and a flood of capital outflows.
Within two months after that crisis passed, the central bank said it was no longer defending T$27.5 -- setting the unit on a long slide that dealers say has yet to play out.

While the central bank has been permitting a slow descent for the currency, its refusal to allow precipitous movements has meant Taiwan's dollar actually has appreciated relative to currencies other than the U.S. dollar, particularly the yen.
"As much as the Taiwan dollar has fallen, if you compare it to the yen, it may still be overvalued," said the first dealer.

From early 1995 when the yen peaked against the U.S. dollar, the Japanese currency has depreciated some 47 percent against the greenback. In the same period, the Taiwan dollar has slid less than eight percent against the U.S. dollar -- even after Wednesday's big slide.

The Taiwan dollar's resulting rise against the yen has contributed to a ballooning of Taiwan's trade deficit with Japan as Taiwan's imports from Japan have become ever cheaper and its exports to Japan more expensive.
In June, the imbalance rose 56.2 percent to US$1.524 billion compared to June 1996.
Dealers have predicted the Taiwan dollar would drop to T$28.5 or even T$29 before seeing a rebound.
"The central bank seems very willing to stay clear of the market at this point," said the first dealer.
"But I don't think it will let the Taiwan dollar fall below T$28.5 as early as, say, tomorrow," she added.
